title: Too Much Aeroplane for One Man
author: Atul Gawande
wiifm: After three days on building individual skill, today brings the correction. Past a certain level of complexity, even brilliant people make dull, avoidable mistakes, and more expertise does not fix it. We follow Atul Gawande, the son of two Indian doctors who became a surgeon and a writer, from an Ohio childhood to the operating theatres of eight cities. His answer to expert error is humbling: a short list read out loud. You will also learn where the evidence wobbles, which matters for anyone who has ever been asked to tick a form on a busy shift.

b: Atul Gawande was born in Brooklyn, New York, in 1965, to two doctors who had come to the United States from India. His father was a urologist and his mother a paediatrician, and when Atul was small the family moved to Athens, a university town in the hills of southeastern Ohio. Medicine was the background noise of his childhood.

He did not go straight into it. He studied biology and political science at Stanford, won a Rhodes scholarship to Oxford to read philosophy, politics and economics, and spent time working in health policy, including on Bill Clinton's 1992 presidential campaign. Only then did he settle on surgery, graduating from Harvard Medical School in 1995 and training as a surgeon in Boston.

In 1998, still a surgical resident, he began writing for The New Yorker. His first book, Complications, came out in 2002 and was unusually honest about the mistakes doctors make. It set the theme for everything that followed. Gawande was not interested in heroic medicine. He was interested in why well-trained, conscientious people, who know exactly what to do, so often fail to do it.
In 2009 he published The Checklist Manifesto. It opens not in a hospital but on an airfield in Ohio, his home state, nearly thirty years before he was born.
ch.cap: Young Atul watches his doctor parents leave at dawn

b: On 30 October 1935, at Wright Field in Dayton, the United States Army Air Corps gathered to watch a competition that everyone thought was already decided. Boeing's entrant, the Model 299, was a gleaming four-engined bomber that could fly faster and further and carry more than anything its rivals offered. A newspaper reporter had dubbed it the flying fortress.

At the controls was Major Ployer Peter Hill, chief of flight testing for the Army's materiel division and a hugely experienced pilot. The aircraft took off, climbed steeply to around three hundred feet, stalled, turned on one wing and crashed in flames. Hill died of his injuries, and so did Boeing's own test pilot, Leslie Tower, who was on board.

The investigation found nothing wrong with the aircraft. Hill had taken off with the gust lock still engaged, a device that clamps the elevator and rudder so the wind cannot batter them on the ground. He had simply forgotten to release it. A newspaper delivered the verdict that nearly killed the project: this was too much aeroplane for one man to fly.

Gawande uses the crash to frame the whole book. Hill was not careless or untrained. He was among the best pilots alive. The aircraft had simply become too complex for even an expert's memory to manage reliably under pressure.
ch.cap: Boeing's Model 299 stalls and falls at Wright Field

b: Gawande borrows a distinction from the philosophers Samuel Gorovitz and Alasdair MacIntyre. When we fail, we fail in one of two ways. Either the knowledge we need does not yet exist, which is an error of ignorance, or the knowledge exists and we did not apply it properly, which they call an error of ineptitude. The word sounds like an insult. It is not. It describes the almost tragic failure of a competent person to do what they demonstrably know.

For most of history, ignorance did nearly all the killing. We did not know what caused infection, so people died of infection. That balance has flipped. Gawande notes that medicine now recognises around thirteen thousand diseases, syndromes and types of injury, and he cites research finding that patients in intensive care need, on average, around a hundred and seventy-eight individual actions a day, each one a chance to slip.

Our know-how, in other words, has outgrown any individual's ability to deliver it reliably. We are not failing because we lack knowledge. We are failing because we cannot consistently carry out the knowledge we already have. Anyone who has worked a busy shift, with a dozen patients, a drug round and an admission arriving, knows exactly what he means.

That is why Gawande's book is not about better doctors. He takes it for granted that most of his colleagues are skilled and conscientious. His question is the more uncomfortable one: why do good people, who know exactly what to do, routinely fail to do it, and what humble device might catch them when they do?
ch.cap: Know-how towers over a nurse on a busy shift

b: After the crash, the Army bought the smaller, cheaper Douglas design instead. But some officers still believed in Boeing's aircraft and arranged to buy a handful for further testing. They faced a practical question. How do you make an aircraft that is too complicated for one person to remember safe for one person to fly?

The obvious answer was more training. But Hill had had all the training anyone could want. So a group of test pilots did something almost comically modest. They wrote a short list of checks to make before take-off, before flight, before landing and after landing, small enough to fit on an index card. Not a manual. Not a course. A card.

With it, Gawande writes, the pilots flew the aircraft some one point eight million miles without a serious accident. The Army eventually ordered thousands of them as the B-17, the bomber that carried much of the American air war over Europe.

The lesson is not that pilots are forgetful. The checklist did not make anyone a better pilot. It took a narrow class of known, stupid, catastrophic errors off the table, so that the pilot's real skill could be spent on everything else.
ch.cap: A test pilot reads the card before take-off

ch.h: Five steps and a nurse's voice
b: In 2001 Peter Pronovost, a critical care specialist at Johns Hopkins Hospital in Baltimore, tried something that sounded too trivial to publish. Central lines, tubes threaded into a large vein in the neck, chest or groin, are routine in intensive care, and a common source of dangerous bloodstream infections. Pronovost wrote down the steps doctors should take when inserting one. There were five: wash your hands, clean the patient's skin with chlorhexidine antiseptic, cover the patient with sterile drapes, wear a sterile mask, hat, gown and gloves, and put a sterile dressing over the site afterwards.

Every doctor knew all five. Pronovost asked the nurses to watch for a month and record what actually happened. In more than a third of cases, doctors skipped at least one step. So he did the second and more important thing. He gave the nurses the authority to stop a doctor who missed a step, with the hospital's backing.

Over the next year, the ten-day line infection rate in that unit fell from eleven per cent to zero. Over fifteen months, by Gawande's account, the unit had just two infections, and the checklist was reckoned to have prevented forty-three infections and eight deaths and saved around two million dollars.

Look at what the intervention really was. It was not the paper. It was a transfer of permission. The list made it legitimate for a nurse to say, out loud, in front of others, that a senior doctor had not cleaned the skin. Anyone who has stood beside a consultant and wondered whether to speak up will feel the weight of that.
ch.cap: A nurse with the checklist may stop the doctor

ch.h: A whole state goes to zero
b: Critics dismissed the Hopkins result in the obvious way: one enthusiastic unit, a charismatic researcher, an effect that would vanish anywhere ordinary. So Pronovost took the idea across a whole state. With the Michigan Health and Hospital Association he launched the Keystone project in intensive care units across Michigan, many of them ordinary community hospitals with thin staffing and no research culture.

The team supplied the checklist, made it the nurses' tool rather than the doctors', and insisted that hospital executives visit the units regularly to hear what frontline staff needed. Within three months, the typical unit's rate of line infections had dropped to zero. Over eighteen months, the project was credited with saving more than fifteen hundred lives and around a hundred and seventy-five million dollars. The results, published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2006, held up when researchers returned later.

Then came the part Gawande clearly finds painful. Hardly anyone rushed to copy it. The intervention cost almost nothing and the evidence was strong, yet uptake was slow. A hospital can buy a surgical robot for millions and advertise it on a billboard. Nobody puts a laminated card on a billboard.
ch.cap: ICUs across Michigan light up as infections hit zero

b: The most useful chapter in the book leaves medicine entirely. Gawande visits the people who put up skyscrapers in Boston, on the reasoning that a tall building is at least as complex as a body, built by hundreds of specialists who may never meet, and yet almost never falls down. Serious building failures in the United States, he reports, are extremely rare.

On the wall of the site office he finds two documents. The first is a construction schedule, the kind of task checklist everyone imagines. The second surprises him. It is a submittal schedule, a list not of tasks but of conversations. It says that by a certain date the structural engineer, the steel contractor and others must have talked to each other about a particular problem and signed off the result. It does not say what they should decide. It says they must confer, and when, and that the conversation must be recorded.

Builders long ago gave up the fantasy of a master builder who holds the whole project in his head. They push decisions out to the people nearest the problem, and use the schedule to force those people to talk at the moments their work collides. Medicine, devoted to the lone heroic expert, had not caught up. A good handover between shifts is exactly this kind of scheduled conversation.
ch.cap: Specialists confer on schedule as a Boston tower rises

b: In 2006 the World Health Organization asked Gawande to lead a programme to cut deaths in surgery worldwide, where hundreds of millions of operations are performed each year. His team drafted a surgical safety checklist and then threw most of it away, because the first versions were too long for anyone to use.

What survived was nineteen items at three pause points: before anaesthesia, before the first cut, and before the patient leaves the theatre. Has the site been marked? Is the pulse oximeter working? Does the patient have a known allergy? Is there a risk of major blood loss? Have antibiotics been given in the last sixty minutes? Are the instrument and swab counts correct? Every item is unremarkable.

The item Gawande valued most was not clinical at all. Before the first incision, everyone in the room says their name and role out loud. Team members in large hospitals often work together without knowing each other's names, and a person who has not spoken at all is less likely to speak up later. Gawande calls this the activation phenomenon: give someone an early chance to speak, and they become more willing to speak again when it matters.

The pilot ran in eight hospitals in eight very different cities: Seattle, Toronto, London, Auckland, Amman, New Delhi, Manila and Ifakara in Tanzania. The results, led by Alex Haynes and published in the New England Journal of Medicine in January 2009, showed deaths falling from one and a half per cent to under one per cent, and major complications from eleven per cent to seven. When staff were asked if they would want the checklist used if they were the patient, ninety-three per cent said yes.
ch.cap: Before the first cut, everyone says their name

b: Here is the part many summaries leave out. In March 2014 the same journal published a study led by David Urbach of what happened when the Canadian province of Ontario made surgical safety checklists mandatory. The sample was enormous: around a hundred hospitals and over two hundred thousand operations before and after. Deaths and complications barely moved, and neither change was statistically significant. On the face of it, the checklist had done nothing.

The honest reading is not that Gawande was wrong. Three things were different. Ontario's hospitals started from a much better baseline, so there was less room to improve. The WHO pilot was coached: teams were trained, observed and helped to adapt the list to their own theatres. And Ontario's version was mandated, with compliance reported by the hospitals themselves.

That is the sharper lesson. The checklist is not the intervention. The conversation it forces is the intervention. Where a list changes how a team talks, who may speak, when and about what, it works. Where it becomes a form ticked on the way past, it does nothing, and staff are right to resent it. A useful test is whether anyone has ever stopped the work because of your checklist. If nothing has ever been halted, you have a form, not a checklist.
ch.cap: Mandated in Ontario, ticked forms gather dust

b: Gawande learned the craft of good checklists from Daniel Boorman, a Boeing engineer who had spent years writing them for pilots. First, choose the type. A read-do list is followed line by line like a recipe, right for emergencies and rare tasks. A do-confirm list is used after the work: the team works from skill and memory, then pauses to confirm the critical items. Most failed checklists are read-do lists forced onto routine work.

Second, keep it short: five to nine items, sixty to ninety seconds. Include only the killer items, the steps that are both most dangerous to skip and most often skipped. Use plain words, tie the pause to a specific moment, and test it in real use, because the first versions will be wrong.

Gawande closes with investors who ran decisions through formal checklists before committing money. One found the list did not improve his best ideas at all. It killed his worst ones. That is the realistic promise. A checklist will not make you brilliant. It raises your floor, and much of what destroys a business, or harms a patient, happens at the floor.

Gawande went on to write Being Mortal in 2014, founded a health research centre called Ariadne Labs, and later served in the American government's global health work. But the idea from that Ohio airfield is the one that has travelled furthest. Skill takes you to the ceiling. A dull little list keeps you off the floor.
ch.cap: A short checklist beside the window raises the floor

take: When something goes wrong, ask whether you lacked the knowledge or failed to apply it. Most failures are now the second kind, and only that kind can be fixed by process.
Once a job has more critical steps than one person can hold under pressure, more skill stops helping and structure starts.
Pronovost's real innovation was letting nurses stop a doctor. Decide who may halt the work using your checklist, and tell them in front of everyone.
Start any briefing with each person stating their name and role. It costs seconds and makes people more likely to speak up later.
Builders fix when specialists must confer, not what they must decide. Put fixed check-ins into projects where certain people must talk and record it.
Include only steps that are most dangerous to skip and most often skipped. A twenty-line list is a manual, and manuals are not read at the moment of risk.
Pick read-do or do-confirm on purpose
Follow line by line for rare or emergency work; work from skill and then confirm for routine work. The wrong choice kills good checklists.
Ontario mandated checklists and saw no measurable change. If your list has never stopped the work, it is a form, not a safety tool.
recall: What caused the 1935 crash of the Boeing Model 299, and what was the response?

Major Hill took off with the gust lock still engaged, locking the controls. Instead of more training, test pilots wrote a short checklist on an index card, and the aircraft went on to become the B-17.
What is the difference between errors of ignorance and errors of ineptitude?
Ignorance means the knowledge needed does not exist; ineptitude means it exists but was not applied. Gawande argues the second now dominates because our know-how has outgrown individual memory.
What was the real innovation in Pronovost's central line checklist?
Giving nurses explicit authority to stop doctors who skipped a step. The transfer of permission, not the paper, cut the unit's ten-day infection rate from eleven per cent to zero.
Why does the WHO checklist ask everyone to say their name and role?
Because of the activation phenomenon: someone who has spoken early is more likely to speak up later when something is wrong. The item gives the room permission to object.
Why did Ontario's mandatory checklist show no significant benefit?

Ontario started from a better baseline, and its rollout was mandated and self-reported rather than coached and adapted. The lesson is that the list only works when it genuinely changes how a team communicates.
note: Based on The Checklist Manifesto and the studies it cites: Pronovost and colleagues in the New England Journal of Medicine, 2006, and Haynes and colleagues in the same journal, 2009. The Ontario challenge is Urbach and colleagues, New England Journal of Medicine, 2014. The 1.8 million miles figure is Gawande's and widely repeated; the 1935 crash and its cause are well documented. Gawande's later career details are from public records.
words: In Gawande's borrowed sense, failing to apply knowledge that already exists, rather than lacking the knowledge.
Major Hill knew to release the gust lock in 1935; his crash was an error of ineptitude, not ignorance.
Caused by medical treatment itself rather than by the original illness.
The bloodstream infections Pronovost targeted were iatrogenic, introduced through central lines that were meant to help.
Done as a routine duty, with minimal care or real attention.
When Ontario mandated checklists, many risked becoming perfunctory forms ticked in passing, which helps explain the null result.
Humble submission to the judgement or authority of someone senior.
Pronovost's checklist worked by overriding the deference that kept nurses silent when a doctor skipped a step.
Action taken in advance to prevent a disease or harm.
One item on the WHO surgical checklist asks whether antibiotic prophylaxis has been given in the sixty minutes before the first cut.
stories: Too much aeroplane for one man

On 30 October 1935, at Wright Field in Dayton, Ohio, the Army gathered to watch Boeing's Model 299, a gleaming four-engined bomber everyone expected to win. At the controls was Major Ployer Peter Hill, one of the most experienced test pilots alive. The aircraft climbed steeply to about three hundred feet, stalled and crashed in flames, killing Hill and Boeing's pilot Leslie Tower. Nothing was wrong with the machine. Hill had forgotten to release the gust lock. A newspaper said it was too much aeroplane for one man to fly. The fix was not more training. It was a checklist on an index card, and the aircraft became the B-17.
Five steps and a nurse's voice

In 2001 Peter Pronovost at Johns Hopkins wrote down five steps for inserting a central line: wash hands, clean the skin with chlorhexidine, drape the patient, wear sterile mask, hat, gown and gloves, and dress the site. Every doctor knew them. He asked nurses to watch for a month, and in more than a third of cases a step was skipped. So he gave nurses the hospital's backing to stop any doctor who missed one. The ten-day infection rate fell from eleven per cent to zero. The real intervention was not the paper. It was permission for a junior person to speak up to a senior one.

In 2007 and 2008 Gawande's WHO team tested a nineteen-item surgical checklist in eight cities, from Seattle and London to Amman and Ifakara in Tanzania. Deaths fell from one and a half per cent to under one per cent. Then in 2014 a study of Ontario, where checklists had been made compulsory across about a hundred hospitals and over two hundred thousand operations, found almost no change. Ontario started from a better baseline, but the deeper difference was that the pilot was coached and adapted, while Ontario's was mandated and self-reported. A list that changes how a team talks saves lives. A list ticked in passing does nothing.
biz: A do-confirm list before a case goes to a lender

Submitting a secured-loan case is routine work done from skill, so use a do-confirm checklist, read aloud at one fixed pause point before submission. Keep it to five to nine killer items, the ones most dangerous to skip and most often skipped, for example: broker status and fees explained and recorded, affordability evidence complete, any vulnerability noted and handled, consent captured, correct lender criteria checked. Give anyone on the team the stated right to halt a case that fails an item. Measure lender returns for missing information, and count how often the list has stopped a case. If it never has, rewrite it.
A read-do card for a client in crisis

On a Debt Support Direct call, a client may mention thoughts of suicide or self-harm. That is rare and high-stakes, exactly where a read-do list beats memory. Agree a short card with your compliance lead: stop the advice conversation, stay calm, ask directly about immediate safety, give the Samaritans number, 116 123, or call 999 if life is at immediate risk, record what happened, and escalate to a named person the same day. Pin it beside every phone and rehearse it quarterly. Measure that every adviser can find and use it in under a minute, and review each real use.
connects: Kahneman praises the Apgar score, a simple checklist of five signs for newborns, as proof that a short formula can beat expert judgement under pressure.
Perrow argues that complex, tightly coupled systems make accidents normal, the same complexity that Gawande says outgrew any single expert's memory.
Clausewitz's friction, the countless small mishaps that make simple things hard in war, is precisely the class of dull error a checklist is built to catch.
recap:
Atul Gawande was born in Brooklyn in nineteen sixty-five to two doctors who had come from India, and grew up in a university town in Ohio. He studied at Stanford and Oxford, worked in health policy, and only then trained as a surgeon in Boston. While still a resident he began writing for The New Yorker, and from the start his subject was uncomfortable. Why do good, well-trained people, who know exactly what to do, so often fail to do it?

His answer begins on an Ohio airfield in nineteen thirty-five. The Army was watching Boeing's new bomber, faster and bigger than anything else. At the controls was one of the most experienced test pilots alive. The plane climbed, stalled and crashed in flames. Nothing was wrong with it. The pilot had forgotten to release a lock on the controls. A newspaper said it was too much aeroplane for one man to fly.

The first big idea is the difference between ignorance and ineptitude. Once, we failed because we did not know enough. Now we mostly fail because we know more than any one person can reliably carry out.

The second idea is how humble the answer is. The test pilots did not order more training. They wrote a list on an index card, and flew the aircraft for well over a million miles without a serious accident.

The third idea is that a checklist transfers permission. In Baltimore, the doctor Peter Pronovost listed five simple steps for inserting a central line, and gave nurses the right to stop any doctor who skipped one. Infections in that unit fell to zero. Across Michigan, the same approach was credited with saving more than fifteen hundred lives.

The fourth idea comes from builders. Skyscraper crews schedule not just tasks but conversations, forcing specialists to talk when their work collides. Gawande's surgical checklist for the World Health Organization even had the team say their names before the first cut, because people who have spoken once speak up again.

Then comes the honest part. When Ontario made checklists compulsory, results barely moved. The list is not the intervention. The conversation it forces is. Where it becomes a form ticked in passing, it does nothing. If your checklist has never stopped the work, it is not a safety tool.

Keep it short, five to nine killer items, and test it in real use.

A checklist will not make you brilliant. It raises your floor, and the floor is where the damage happens.
